_about: Common procedures and operations: why they are done, what happens, recovery and risks, linked to the anatomy involved. Educational; individual advice comes from the treating team.

categories.name: Operations
categories.summary: Procedures done under anaesthetic in an operating theatre.

categories.name: Heart procedures
categories.summary: Catheter and surgical treatments for the heart and coronary arteries.

categories.name: Endoscopic procedures
categories.summary: Looking and treating inside the body through a scope.

categories.name: Bedside procedures
categories.summary: Procedures done in clinic or on the ward with local anaesthetic or none.

appendectomy.name: Appendicectomy
appendectomy.what: Removal of the inflamed appendix, the blind-ended tube hanging off the caecum at the start of the large intestine. Usually done through three small keyhole incisions with a camera (laparoscopically), occasionally through a single cut in the right lower abdomen.
why: Acute appendicitis, to prevent perforation and peritonitis
An appendix mass or abscess after initial antibiotics and drainage
Occasionally, an appendix tumour found on imaging or during other surgery
before: Blood tests, pregnancy test in women, sometimes ultrasound or CT
Nil by mouth; intravenous fluids and antibiotics
Consent and marking; general anaesthetic
steps: Carbon dioxide inflates the abdomen through a port at the navel to create working space
A camera and two instruments are introduced through 5-12 mm ports
The appendix is lifted, its blood supply in the mesoappendix sealed, and its base tied or stapled at the caecum
The appendix is removed in a bag; any pus is washed out
Ports are removed and the small wounds closed with dissolvable stitches
after: Home the same or next day for uncomplicated cases
Simple painkillers; walk early
Antibiotics continued for a few days if the appendix had perforated
appendectomy.recovery: Back to desk work in about a week and to sport in two to four weeks after keyhole surgery; longer after open surgery or a perforated appendix.
risks: Wound infection (more after perforation)
Pelvic abscess
Bleeding, injury to bowel or bladder (rare)
Stump leak, adhesions, hernia at the port site (rare)
Anaesthetic risks
alternatives: Antibiotics alone for uncomplicated appendicitis: works in most short term, but about a third need surgery within a few years
Drainage and delayed surgery for an abscess

cholecystectomy.name: Cholecystectomy
cholecystectomy.what: Removal of the gallbladder, the small sac under the liver that stores bile. The commonest planned abdominal operation, almost always done by keyhole surgery. The liver keeps making bile, which then flows straight into the duodenum.
why: Gallstones causing repeated pain (biliary colic)
Acute cholecystitis (an inflamed, infected gallbladder)
Gallstone pancreatitis, once recovered, to prevent recurrence
Gallbladder polyps above 10 mm or a porcelain gallbladder (cancer risk)
before: Ultrasound confirming stones; liver function tests; MRCP or ERCP if stones are suspected in the bile duct
Fasting; general anaesthetic
Antibiotics at induction if inflamed
steps: Four ports: one at the navel for the camera, three under the right ribs
The gallbladder is retracted upward to expose Calot's triangle
The cystic duct and cystic artery are identified with a 'critical view of safety', clipped and divided
The gallbladder is peeled off the liver bed with diathermy and removed in a bag through the navel port
An X-ray of the bile duct (cholangiogram) may be done during the operation
after: Home the same day or next morning
Shoulder-tip pain from residual gas for a day or two
Normal diet resumed; some people notice looser stools after fatty meals
cholecystectomy.recovery: Most people return to normal activities within two weeks; heavy lifting avoided for a few weeks.
risks: Bile leak from the liver bed or cystic duct stump (1-2%)
Injury to the common bile duct (about 1 in 300), the serious complication
Bleeding, infection, retained stones in the duct
Conversion to open surgery (a few per cent, more in acute inflammation)
alternatives: Watchful waiting for stones with no symptoms
Antibiotics and a drainage tube (cholecystostomy) in patients too unwell for surgery
Bile-acid tablets for tiny stones (slow, often recur)

knee-replacement.name: Knee replacement
knee-replacement.what: The worn surfaces at the end of the femur and top of the tibia are cut away and capped with metal components, with a polyethylene insert between them as the new cartilage; the back of the kneecap is often resurfaced. A partial replacement treats one compartment only when the rest of the joint is healthy.
why: Severe osteoarthritis (or rheumatoid arthritis) with pain that limits walking, sleep and daily life despite painkillers, physiotherapy, weight loss and injections
Post-traumatic arthritis after fractures
Rarely, tumours or failed previous surgery
before: Standing X-rays; blood tests, ECG, MRSA screen, dental check
'Joint school' education, prehabilitation exercises, weight optimisation
Spinal or general anaesthetic with nerve blocks
steps: A vertical incision over the front of the knee; the kneecap is moved aside
Guided cuts remove a few millimetres from the end of the femur and top of the tibia, and worn cartilage and the cruciate ligaments as required
Trial components are fitted and the ligament balance and alignment checked through the full range of movement
The final metal components are cemented (or press-fitted) and the plastic insert locked in
The joint is washed, local anaesthetic infiltrated, and the layers closed
after: Standing and walking with a frame the same day or next
Physiotherapy from day one: bending, straightening, stairs; home in 1-3 days
Blood-thinning injections or tablets for 2-6 weeks; ice and elevation
Wound check at two weeks; six-week and one-year reviews
knee-replacement.recovery: Walking without aids by about six weeks, driving at 6-8 weeks, most of the benefit by three months and continued improvement for a year. A knee replacement usually lasts 15-25 years.
risks: Deep infection (about 1%), the most serious, sometimes needing revision
Blood clots in the leg or lung
Stiffness needing manipulation
Loosening or wear over time; a small number never feel quite right
Nerve or vessel injury, fracture around the implant (rare)
alternatives: Exercise programmes, weight loss, walking aids, bracing
Steroid or hyaluronic acid injections
Osteotomy (realigning the bone) in younger patients with one-sided wear
Arthroscopy is not helpful for degenerative knees

cataract-surgery.name: Cataract surgery
cataract-surgery.what: The cloudy natural lens of the eye is broken up with ultrasound through a 2-3 mm incision at the edge of the cornea and sucked out, and a folded plastic lens is injected into the empty lens capsule where it unfolds. Done under drops or a local anaesthetic injection in 15-30 minutes, it is the commonest operation in the world.
why: A cataract that blurs vision or causes glare enough to affect daily life, driving or work
Rarely, to see the retina for treating diabetic eye disease, or to lower eye pressure in glaucoma
before: Eye measurements (biometry) to choose the lens power, aiming for distance or near focus
Drops to dilate the pupil on the day; anaesthetic drops or a small injection
No need to fast for local anaesthetic; regular medicines continued
steps: A tiny self-sealing incision is made at the edge of the cornea
A circular opening is torn in the front of the lens capsule
An ultrasound probe emulsifies the lens nucleus, which is aspirated along with the softer cortex
The folded intraocular lens is injected into the capsule and unfolds into place
The incision seals without stitches; antibiotic is placed in the eye
after: Home within an hour with a clear shield to wear at night for a week
Antibiotic and anti-inflammatory drops for about four weeks
Vision usually clears within days; new glasses after 4-6 weeks
Avoid rubbing the eye, swimming and heavy lifting for a couple of weeks
cataract-surgery.recovery: Most people see well within a few days and resume driving within one to two weeks once the eye meets the standard. The second eye is done weeks later.
risks: Posterior capsule opacification (cloudy membrane behind the lens) in up to a fifth over years, cleared with a quick laser
Infection inside the eye (endophthalmitis, about 1 in 1000), sight-threatening
Tear of the capsule, retinal detachment, swelling of the retina, raised pressure
A refractive surprise needing glasses or a lens exchange
alternatives: Stronger glasses and better lighting while the cataract is mild
No surgery, if vision is acceptable; cataracts do not damage the eye by waiting except when very advanced

angioplasty.name: Coronary angioplasty and stenting
angioplasty.what: A narrowed or blocked coronary artery is opened from inside. A fine wire is steered across the narrowing through a catheter from the wrist or groin, a balloon is inflated to crush the plaque against the wall, and a drug-coated metal mesh stent is expanded to hold the artery open. As primary PCI it is the emergency treatment for a heart attack; electively it relieves angina.
why: ST-elevation heart attack (STEMI): open the artery within 120 minutes of diagnosis
Non-ST-elevation heart attack and unstable angina, usually within days
Stable angina not controlled by medication, or with a large area of ischaemia on testing

structures: Circumflex branch of left coronary artery
Diagonal branch of anterior descending branch of left coronary artery
Posterior interventricular branch of right coronary artery
Marginal branch of right coronary artery

before: ECG, troponin, kidney function, clotting; a loading dose of aspirin and a second antiplatelet
Nil by mouth if elective; in an emergency straight to the catheter lab
Local anaesthetic to the wrist; mild sedation
steps: A sheath is placed in the radial (or femoral) artery and heparin given
Catheters are passed to the origin of each coronary artery and contrast injected to map the narrowings
A guidewire is steered across the lesion
A balloon is inflated for seconds to open the narrowing, with the ECG watched for ischaemia
A drug-eluting stent on a balloon is positioned and expanded to the artery's size; a final angiogram confirms flow
The sheath is removed and the wrist compressed with a band
after: Bed rest for a few hours (longer for femoral access); home the next day for elective cases, 2-3 days after a heart attack
Dual antiplatelet therapy for 6-12 months to stop clot forming on the stent, then aspirin for life
Statin, beta blocker and ACE inhibitor as indicated; cardiac rehabilitation
angioplasty.recovery: Back to light activity within days and work in a week or two for elective procedures; after a heart attack, structured rehabilitation over 6-12 weeks.
risks: Bruising or bleeding at the puncture site; rarely damage to the artery
Contrast kidney injury and allergy
Heart attack, stroke or death during the procedure (well under 1% electively, higher in emergencies)
Stent thrombosis (rare, but serious if antiplatelets are stopped early); restenosis within the stent over years
Emergency bypass surgery (rare)
alternatives: Medication alone for stable angina (equally good for survival in many cases)
Coronary artery bypass grafting for three-vessel or left main disease, especially with diabetes
Thrombolysis (clot-busting drugs) when PCI cannot be delivered in time

references.title: NHS: Coronary angioplasty and stent insertion

coronary-bypass.name: Coronary artery bypass grafting
coronary-bypass.what: Open-heart surgery that routes blood around blocked coronary arteries using the patient's own vessels: the internal mammary artery from inside the chest wall is joined beyond the blockage in the left anterior descending artery, and lengths of leg vein or radial artery bridge from the aorta to the other vessels. Usually done on a heart-lung machine with the heart stopped.
why: Left main stem or three-vessel coronary disease, particularly with diabetes or a weak ventricle
Angina not controlled by medication where anatomy is unsuitable for stents
Failed or complicated angioplasty
Combined with valve surgery when both are needed

structures: Diagonal branch of anterior descending branch of left coronary artery
Circumflex branch of left coronary artery
Posterior interventricular branch of right coronary artery

before: Coronary angiography and echocardiogram; carotid ultrasound; lung function, bloods, dental review
Stop clopidogrel a few days before; continue aspirin
General anaesthetic; arterial and central venous lines; urinary catheter
steps: The sternum is split lengthways and the internal mammary artery harvested from the chest wall while the vein is taken from the leg
Heparin is given and the heart-lung machine takes over circulation; the aorta is clamped and the heart arrested with cold potassium solution
Each graft is sewn with fine sutures to the coronary artery beyond its blockage; vein grafts are then joined to the aorta
The heart is restarted, the machine weaned off, and pacing wires and chest drains placed
The sternum is closed with steel wires and the skin closed
after: Intensive care overnight on a ventilator for a few hours, then the ward; 5-8 days in hospital
Chest drains out in a day or two; pain from the sternum and leg wound
Aspirin, statin, beta blocker; cardiac rehabilitation from about six weeks
coronary-bypass.recovery: Six to twelve weeks off work, no driving for four weeks, no heavy lifting for three months while the sternum knits; full benefit at about three months. Arterial grafts last decades; vein grafts about half are narrowed by ten years.
risks: Death (around 1-2% electively, higher in emergencies and with other illness)
Stroke (1-2%), heart attack, kidney injury
Atrial fibrillation in a third (usually temporary)
Wound infection, especially of the sternum in diabetes and obesity
Bleeding needing a return to theatre; memory and concentration changes for some months
alternatives: Angioplasty and stents for suitable anatomy
Optimal medical therapy
Off-pump and minimally invasive bypass in selected cases

cardiac-catheterization.name: Cardiac catheterisation
cardiac-catheterization.what: Thin tubes are passed through an artery or vein to the heart to measure pressures and oxygen levels in its chambers, inject contrast into the coronary arteries and chambers, and, in electrophysiology studies, map the electrical circuits and burn or freeze the tissue causing an arrhythmia (ablation).
why: Mapping coronary artery narrowing in angina or after a heart attack (before angioplasty or bypass)
Assessing valve disease and heart failure by measuring pressures, including pulmonary hypertension
Diagnosing and ablating arrhythmias such as atrial fibrillation, SVT and atrial flutter
Closing holes in the heart, replacing valves through a catheter (TAVI), biopsy of heart muscle
before: Blood tests including kidney function and clotting; ECG; sometimes echo or CT
Fasting 4-6 hours; metformin and blood thinners managed
Local anaesthetic to the wrist or groin, light sedation; awake throughout
steps: A sheath is placed in the radial artery (coronaries), femoral artery (left heart) or femoral vein (right heart, electrophysiology)
Catheters are advanced under X-ray screening to the coronary origins or heart chambers
Contrast injections film the arteries from several angles; pressures are recorded through the catheter
In electrophysiology, several electrode catheters map the rhythm; pacing provokes the arrhythmia and the culprit tissue is ablated
Sheaths are removed and the site compressed or closed with a plug
after: Lie flat for 2-6 hours after femoral access; a wrist band for radial
Home the same day for diagnostic studies; drink fluids to clear contrast
Results explained immediately with a plan for medication, stents or surgery
cardiac-catheterization.recovery: Normal activities within a day or two; avoid heavy lifting for a week. Ablation for atrial fibrillation is followed by anticoagulation for at least two months.
risks: Bruising, bleeding or a false aneurysm at the puncture site
Contrast kidney injury or allergy
Stroke, heart attack, arrhythmia, perforation of the heart (all rare, well under 1%)
For ablation: damage to the heart's normal conduction needing a pacemaker (rare)
alternatives: CT coronary angiography for stable chest pain (no catheter, but no treatment possible)
Echocardiography and cardiac MRI for structure and function
Medication for arrhythmias instead of ablation

upper-endoscopy.name: Gastroscopy
upper-endoscopy.what: A thin flexible camera is passed through the mouth down the oesophagus, into the stomach and the first part of the small intestine, giving a direct view of the lining and allowing biopsies and treatment. It takes 5-15 minutes with throat spray or light sedation.
why: Difficulty or pain on swallowing, persistent indigestion, especially over 55 or with weight loss
Vomiting blood or black stools (urgent, to find and treat the bleeding point)
Unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia
Diagnosing coeliac disease, H. pylori, Barrett oesophagus; surveillance of ulcers and Barrett
Treatment: stretching strictures, removing polyps, banding varices, placing feeding tubes and stents
before: Nothing to eat for 6 hours and clear fluids only until 2 hours before
Stop acid-suppressing tablets for two weeks if testing for H. pylori or ulcers is the aim
Blood thinners managed; a driver if sedated
steps: Lying on the left side with a mouthguard; throat spray numbs the gullet, or sedation is given through a cannula
The scope is swallowed over the back of the tongue and advanced under direct vision
Air inflates the stomach for a clear view; the oesophagus, stomach and duodenum are inspected in turn
Biopsies are taken painlessly with forceps through the scope; polyps removed, bleeding treated with clips, injections or heat
The scope is withdrawn; the whole procedure is recorded
after: Sore throat and bloating for a day
Eat and drink once the throat spray has worn off (about an hour)
No driving, alcohol or important decisions for 24 hours after sedation
Biopsy results in one to two weeks
upper-endoscopy.recovery: Normal activities the same day (next day after sedation).
risks: Sore throat, bloating
Bleeding after biopsy or polyp removal (small)
Perforation of the oesophagus or stomach (about 1 in 3000, higher with stretching)
Reaction to sedation, chest infection from aspiration (rare)
alternatives: Barium swallow or CT (no biopsies)
Capsule endoscopy for the small bowel
A trial of acid suppression in younger patients without alarm features

colonoscopy.name: Colonoscopy
colonoscopy.what: A flexible camera is passed through the anus around the whole large intestine to the caecum and often into the last part of the small intestine. Polyps found on the way are removed, which prevents them growing into cancer; this is why screening colonoscopy reduces bowel cancer deaths.
why: A positive stool screening test (FIT) or bleeding from the bowel
Change in bowel habit, unexplained weight loss or iron-deficiency anaemia
Diagnosing and monitoring inflammatory bowel disease
Surveillance after polyps or bowel cancer, and in high-risk families
Removing polyps, stopping bleeding, dilating strictures, decompressing a twisted bowel
before: Low-fibre diet for a few days, then strong laxative bowel preparation the day before, drinking litres of clear fluid until the output runs clear
Iron tablets stopped a week before; blood thinners and diabetes medicines adjusted
Sedation and painkiller through a cannula, or gas and air
steps: Lying on the left side; the lubricated scope is inserted and advanced with carbon dioxide inflating the bowel
The scope is steered around the sigmoid, descending, transverse and ascending colon to the caecum, changing position or with abdominal pressure to straighten loops
The lining is inspected carefully on the slow withdrawal (at least six minutes)
Polyps are snared with a wire loop and cut with diathermy, or removed cold if small; larger lesions lifted and resected in pieces
Biopsies are taken from any abnormal or inflamed areas
after: Wind and cramps for a few hours as gas passes
Eat and drink normally; a little blood after polypectomy is expected
No driving for 24 hours after sedation
Histology in one to two weeks decides surveillance intervals
risks: Bleeding after polyp removal (about 1 in 100 for large polyps, sometimes delayed by a week)
Perforation (about 1 in 1000-2000), more after resection of large polyps; may need surgery
Missed lesions (some per cent, especially with poor preparation)
Reaction to sedation; dehydration from bowel preparation in the frail
alternatives: CT colonography (virtual colonoscopy): no sedation, but no biopsies and needs colonoscopy if abnormal
Flexible sigmoidoscopy: examines only the left colon with an enema
Capsule colonoscopy in selected cases

bronchoscopy.name: Bronchoscopy
bronchoscopy.what: A thin flexible scope is passed through the nose or mouth, between the vocal cords and down the trachea into the bronchi of each lung, to inspect the airways, wash out or brush cells, and take biopsies. Endobronchial ultrasound (EBUS) adds an ultrasound probe on the scope tip so lymph nodes beside the airways can be sampled with a needle through the wall.
why: A lung mass or shadow on CT, to diagnose and stage lung cancer
Coughing up blood
Persistent infection or collapse of a lung segment; sampling in immunosuppressed patients
Removing inhaled foreign bodies and mucus plugs; placing airway stents
Diagnosing sarcoidosis, tuberculosis and interstitial lung disease (cryobiopsy)

structures: Left anterior basal segmental bronchial tree

before: CT of the chest; clotting and blood count; spirometry and oxygen level
Fasting 4-6 hours; blood thinners managed
Local anaesthetic spray to the nose and throat plus sedation; oxygen through the nose; monitoring throughout
steps: The scope passes through the nostril, over the back of the tongue, and lidocaine is sprayed onto the vocal cords before passing between them
The trachea and the bronchial tree of both lungs are inspected to segmental level
Saline washings (lavage) are instilled and suctioned for microbiology and cytology; brushings scrape cells from a lesion
Forceps biopsies are taken from visible tumours; transbronchial biopsies from lung tissue beyond view, sometimes under X-ray guidance
With EBUS, a needle passes through the airway wall into lymph nodes under ultrasound view
after: Nothing to eat or drink until the throat numbness wears off (1-2 hours)
Mild cough, sore throat, a little blood-streaked sputum for a day
A chest X-ray if transbronchial biopsies were taken, to check for a collapsed lung
No driving for 24 hours; results in a week or two
risks: Low oxygen and breathlessness during the procedure
Bleeding, usually minor
Pneumothorax (collapsed lung) after transbronchial biopsy (a few per cent)
Fever, infection, arrhythmia, laryngospasm (rare)
alternatives: CT-guided needle biopsy through the chest wall for peripheral lesions
Sputum cytology and blood tests
Surgical biopsy (mediastinoscopy, VATS)

dialysis.name: Dialysis
dialysis.what: Artificial replacement of the kidneys' filtering work when they have failed. In haemodialysis, blood is pumped from a vascular access through a filter where waste and excess water pass across a membrane into dialysis fluid, then returned, usually for four hours three times a week. In peritoneal dialysis, fluid is run into the abdomen through a permanent catheter and the peritoneum itself acts as the membrane, exchanged several times a day or overnight by a machine.
why: End-stage kidney disease (eGFR under about 10, or symptoms of uraemia, fluid overload or high potassium that medication cannot control)
Acute kidney injury with life-threatening potassium, acidosis, fluid overload or toxins
Some poisonings (lithium, methanol, aspirin overdose)
before: Months of planning in advanced kidney disease: education, choosing the type, vaccination against hepatitis B

Creating access: an arteriovenous fistula joining the radial artery and cephalic vein at the wrist (or a graft), which needs 6-12 weeks to mature; or a tunnelled catheter in the internal jugular vein for urgent starts
For peritoneal dialysis, a catheter placed into the abdomen two weeks before use
steps: Haemodialysis: two needles in the fistula (or the catheter connected); blood flows at 300-400 mL/min through the dialyser; heparin prevents clotting; the machine removes a set volume of fluid; weight, blood pressure and bloods are monitored

Peritoneal dialysis: 2 litres of warmed glucose-based fluid drains into the abdomen, dwells for hours while waste and water diffuse across the peritoneum, then drains out; repeated 4 times a day (CAPD) or by a cycler overnight (APD)
Diet restricts potassium, phosphate, salt and fluid; phosphate binders, erythropoietin and vitamin D replace kidney functions dialysis cannot
after: Tiredness and cramps after haemodialysis sessions are common
Regular monthly bloods, adequacy checks and fistula care
Assessment for a kidney transplant, which offers the best survival and quality of life
dialysis.recovery: Dialysis is ongoing rather than a one-off procedure; many people continue work and travel, with peritoneal or home haemodialysis giving more flexibility.
risks: Low blood pressure, cramps, nausea during sessions
Access problems: fistula clotting or narrowing, catheter infection and bloodstream infection
Peritonitis in peritoneal dialysis (about one episode every 2-3 years)
Long term: cardiovascular disease, bone disease, amyloid, anaemia; life expectancy is reduced compared with transplantation
alternatives: Kidney transplantation (living or deceased donor), pre-emptively where possible
Conservative kidney management: symptom control without dialysis, chosen by some frail or elderly patients

blood-transfusion.name: Blood transfusion
blood-transfusion.what: Donated blood components given into a vein: red cells for anaemia and blood loss, platelets for low counts with bleeding, fresh frozen plasma and cryoprecipitate for clotting factor deficiency. Each unit is matched to the recipient's ABO and RhD blood groups and screened for antibodies, and identity is checked at every step.
why: Major bleeding from trauma, surgery, the gut or childbirth
Symptomatic anaemia that cannot wait for iron or other treatment; haemoglobin below about 70 g/L in stable patients (80 in heart disease)
Bone marrow failure and chemotherapy
Sickle cell disease and thalassaemia (regular transfusions)
Reversing clotting problems before surgery or in massive haemorrhage
before: A group-and-save or crossmatch sample, labelled at the bedside from a wristband check
Consent, explaining benefits, risks and alternatives; baseline temperature, pulse and blood pressure
A cannula in a forearm vein
steps: Two staff check the unit against the patient's identity and the compatibility label
Red cells run over 1.5-3 hours (faster in emergencies); platelets over 30 minutes; plasma over 30-60 minutes
Observations are repeated at 15 minutes and at the end of each unit
Any fever, rash, breathlessness or pain stops the transfusion immediately for assessment
Haemoglobin is rechecked after; each unit of red cells raises it by about 10 g/L
after: Most people feel better within hours if anaemia was symptomatic
Delayed reactions (jaundice, falling haemoglobin) can occur a week or so later
Women of childbearing age receive RhD-matched and K-negative blood to protect future pregnancies
blood-transfusion.recovery: Usually a day-case or in-patient treatment with no recovery period of its own.
risks: Mild fever or hives (about 1 in 100)
Fluid overload in the elderly and heart failure (the commonest serious harm), prevented by slow rates and diuretics
Acute haemolytic reaction from a wrong-blood error (rare but can be fatal), why identity checks are strict
Transfusion-related acute lung injury, bacterial contamination of platelets, and iron overload with repeated transfusion
Infection transmission is extremely rare with modern screening (HIV about 1 in several million)
alternatives: Iron (oral or intravenous), B12, folate and erythropoietin for anaemia with time to respond
Tranexamic acid and cell salvage in surgery to reduce the need
Patient blood management: correcting anaemia before planned surgery

urinary-catheterization.name: Urinary catheterisation
urinary-catheterization.what: A soft tube passed along the urethra into the bladder to drain urine, held in place by a small balloon inflated inside the bladder. Used for hours during surgery, days on a ward, or long term when the bladder cannot empty. A suprapubic catheter enters through the lower abdominal wall instead; intermittent catheterisation passes a tube several times a day and removes it each time.
why: Acute urinary retention (usually from an enlarged prostate) or chronic retention with kidney damage
Measuring urine output hour by hour in critical illness and major surgery
Neurological bladder problems (spinal cord injury, multiple sclerosis), often by self-catheterisation
Bladder irrigation after prostate or bladder surgery, or with clots
Incontinence with skin breakdown when other measures fail (last resort)
before: Explanation and consent; checking for latex allergy and previous difficult catheters
Sterile technique: hand hygiene, gloves, cleaning the urethral opening
Anaesthetic lubricant gel instilled into the urethra and left for a few minutes
steps: The catheter (usually 12-16 Fr) is advanced gently along the urethra; in women the short urethra opens just above the vagina, and in men the penis is held upright to straighten the first bend, then lowered to pass the prostate
Urine flows once the tip is in the bladder; the catheter is advanced further before the balloon is inflated with 10 mL of sterile water
It is drawn back until the balloon rests at the bladder neck and connected to a drainage bag or valve
The volume drained is recorded; very large volumes are drained in stages if chronic retention is suspected
The catheter is secured to the thigh to prevent traction
after: Daily cleaning of the meatus, keeping the bag below bladder level and changing bags on schedule
Removal (trial without catheter) as soon as it is no longer needed, usually within days
Long-term catheters are changed every 4-12 weeks; bacteria in the urine are expected and not treated unless there are symptoms
urinary-catheterization.recovery: Slight stinging on first passing urine after removal is normal; a failed trial without catheter leads to re-catheterisation and urology review.
risks: Urinary tract infection, rising with each day in place, and catheter-related sepsis
Urethral trauma, bleeding and false passage, especially in men with strictures or enlarged prostates
Blockage by debris or clots; bypassing; bladder spasm
Long term: strictures, stones, bladder cancer risk after many years
alternatives: Bladder scan and watchful measures for mild retention
Alpha-blocker tablets before a trial without catheter in prostatic retention
Intermittent self-catheterisation or suprapubic catheter for long-term needs
Sheath (condom) drainage or pads for incontinence

joint-aspiration.name: Joint aspiration and injection
joint-aspiration.what: A needle is passed into a swollen joint to draw off fluid for analysis and to relieve pressure, often followed by an injection of corticosteroid and local anaesthetic through the same needle to settle inflammation. The knee is the commonest site; the shoulder, wrist, elbow, ankle and hip (with ultrasound guidance) are also done.
why: A hot, swollen joint where septic arthritis must be ruled out (the fluid goes for urgent microscopy and culture)
Diagnosing gout and pseudogout by finding crystals under polarised light
Relieving a tense, painful effusion after injury or in osteoarthritis
Steroid injection for osteoarthritis flares, rheumatoid arthritis, frozen shoulder, bursitis and tendon sheath inflammation
before: Explain and consent; check for anticoagulants (not a contraindication for most joints), skin infection over the site, and allergy
Position the joint: the knee slightly bent over a roll; the landmark chosen beside the patella
Skin cleaned with antiseptic; sterile gloves; local anaesthetic to the skin optional
steps: A needle (18-21 gauge) on a syringe is advanced through the skin into the joint space using landmarks or ultrasound, with a giving-way as it enters
Fluid is aspirated: its colour and clarity noted (clear yellow, cloudy, bloody, pus)
Samples are sent for cell count, Gram stain and culture, and crystal examination
If indicated, the syringe is swapped and steroid (for example 40 mg methylprednisolone or triamcinolone) with lidocaine is injected
The needle is withdrawn and a dressing applied; the fluid volume is recorded
after: Rest the joint for 24-48 hours after a steroid injection; ice for discomfort
Watch for a flare of pain in the first day (crystal reaction to the steroid) and for redness, fever or increasing pain suggesting infection
Diabetics: blood glucose may rise for a few days
joint-aspiration.recovery: Relief from an aspiration is immediate; steroid benefit builds over a few days and lasts weeks to months.
risks: Introducing infection into the joint (about 1 in 10,000 with sterile technique)
Bleeding into the joint, especially on anticoagulants
Post-injection flare, skin thinning or pale patch at the site, facial flushing
Cartilage damage with repeated steroid injections (limit to 3-4 a year)
alternatives: Oral anti-inflammatories and rest
Physiotherapy and bracing
Ultrasound-guided injection for deep or difficult joints
Arthroscopy for mechanical problems

caesarean-section.name: Caesarean section
caesarean-section.what: Birth of a baby through a cut in the lower abdomen and in the lower segment of the uterus, usually under a spinal or epidural anaesthetic so that the person is awake and a birth partner can be present. The operation is the same for trans men and non-binary people who give birth. It is one of the commonest operations carried out in the UK and accounts for a substantial proportion of births. A planned (elective) caesarean is booked in advance, normally after 39 weeks; an unplanned one is done during pregnancy or labour, and its urgency ranges from an immediate threat to the life of the woman or the baby, when the baby is delivered within minutes, to a decision that can wait for the next available theatre. Urgency is graded in four categories, from an immediate threat to life through to a caesarean timed to suit the woman and the team.
why: The baby lies breech or across the uterus, or turning the baby by external cephalic version has not worked or is not suitable
The placenta covers or lies close to the cervix (placenta praevia), or is abnormally attached to the scar of an earlier caesarean
A twin or higher-order pregnancy where the first baby is not head-down, or where labour is not thought to be safe
Concern about the baby during labour, such as an abnormal heart rate pattern, bleeding from the placenta or a cord prolapse
Labour that does not progress, or a baby in a position that cannot pass through the pelvis
Maternal conditions such as severe pre-eclampsia, and some infections that could be passed to the baby during a vaginal birth

A previous caesarean, where a planned repeat operation is chosen rather than a vaginal birth after caesarean, or a request for a caesarean birth after the risks and benefits of both routes have been discussed
before: A discussion of the reasons, the risks of caesarean and of vaginal birth, and what the recovery involves, with written consent
A blood count and a group and save sample, with anaemia treated beforehand where there is time; an ultrasound to confirm the position of the baby and the placenta
Fasting and a medicine to reduce stomach acid, because of the small risk of acid entering the lungs under anaesthetic
A spinal or epidural anaesthetic in most cases, with a general anaesthetic kept for the most urgent operations or when a regional block is not possible
Antibiotics before the skin is cut, clot-prevention stockings, and a catheter passed once the anaesthetic is working
steps: The anaesthetic is tested to make sure the abdomen is numb, the skin is cleaned and draped, and a screen is placed so that the birth can still be watched if the parents wish

A transverse incision is made a little above the pubic bone and deepened to the rectus sheath, which is opened and lifted; the rectus muscles are separated in the midline, keeping clear of the inferior epigastric vessels at their outer edges, and the peritoneum is opened
The fold of peritoneum over the lower segment of the uterus is incised and the bladder is gently pushed downwards out of the way

A small transverse cut is made in the lower segment and opened out with the fingers; the membranes are ruptured and the head, or the breech, is delivered with a hand and pressure on the fundus, occasionally helped by forceps or a vacuum cup

The cord is clamped, after a short delay when the baby is well, and a drug that contracts the uterus is given so that the placenta separates and is delivered by controlled traction on the cord; the cavity is checked to be empty
The uterine incision is closed, normally in two layers, bleeding is checked, swabs and instruments are counted, the sheath is closed and the skin is closed with a suture or clips

A vertical (classical) incision in the uterus is used only occasionally, for example at very early gestations or when the lower segment cannot be reached safely, and it changes the advice about future births
after: Skin-to-skin contact and the first feed usually start in theatre or in recovery, with help to find a position that keeps the baby off the wound

The catheter comes out once the anaesthetic has worn off and walking, eating and drinking start early; regular pain relief is given and clot-prevention injections continue for a period after discharge
The dressing is removed after a day or two and the wound is kept clean and dry; clips or non-absorbable stitches are taken out by a midwife

Vaginal bleeding (lochia) continues for a few weeks, as it does after any birth; bleeding that becomes heavy again or passes large clots, offensive-smelling discharge, fever, a severe headache with visual disturbance, calf pain or breathlessness are reported to the maternity unit or NHS 111 straight away
caesarean-section.recovery: Most people stay in hospital for one to two days and feel a little stronger each week over about six weeks. Driving restarts when an emergency stop can be done comfortably, and lifting anything heavier than the baby is avoided at first. The scar sits low and fades over about a year; numbness around it is common and usually improves.
risks: Infection of the wound, the lining of the uterus or the urine, and heavier bleeding than at a vaginal birth, occasionally needing a transfusion
Venous thromboembolism (deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism), which is why clot prevention and early walking matter
Injury to the bladder, and less often to the ureter or bowel, which is more likely when there are adhesions from previous surgery
A small cut to the baby's skin at the time of delivery, and a greater chance of short-lived breathing difficulty in the baby, which is less common after 39 weeks
Effects on later pregnancies: a placenta lying low or growing into the scar, and a small risk of the scar giving way in a future labour
A longer recovery than an uncomplicated vaginal birth, and adhesions that can make later abdominal surgery harder
Uncommonly, further surgery is needed, including removal of the uterus (hysterectomy) if bleeding cannot be controlled by other means
alternatives: Vaginal birth, including a planned vaginal birth after a previous caesarean once the risks have been discussed
Induction of labour where the concern is about continuing the pregnancy rather than about labour itself
An assisted vaginal birth with forceps or a vacuum cup when the cervix is fully dilated and the head is low enough
External cephalic version to turn a breech baby head-down before labour

chest-masculinisation.name: Chest masculinisation (top surgery)
chest-masculinisation.what: Removal of most of the breast tissue and excess skin, with resizing and repositioning of the nipples, to give a flat chest with a male contour; a common gender-affirming operation for trans men and non-binary people assigned female at birth. It is not the same as a mastectomy for cancer: a thin layer of tissue is deliberately left for an even contour, so a small amount of breast tissue remains. The complementary operation for trans women, breast augmentation, places implants under or over the pectoralis major once oestrogen-driven breast growth has settled. Gender incongruence is not a mental illness: the World Health Organization classifies it under conditions related to sexual health, and chest surgery is one option that some, not all, trans people choose.
why: Gender incongruence in trans men and non-binary people who want a flat, masculine chest, after assessment under the WPATH Standards of Care; hormone therapy is not a prerequisite
Relief from long-term chest binding, which can cause skin damage, rib and back pain and restricted breathing
Breast augmentation for trans women whose breast growth on oestrogen is less than they want, usually judged once growth has largely stopped, which commonly takes two to three years of hormone therapy

structures: Sternocostal part of left pectoralis major
Sternocostal part of right pectoralis major

before: Assessment by a gender identity service following the WPATH Standards of Care: a settled decision and capacity to consent; testosterone is not required, although many people are taking it

Stopping smoking, which impairs nipple graft and wound healing, and weight optimised; breast imaging (mammography or ultrasound) beforehand where the surgeon's protocol or age, a family history of breast cancer or a lump warrants it
Choice of technique from chest size and skin elasticity: periareolar or keyhole for small chests with elastic skin, double incision with free nipple grafts for larger chests or loose skin
Markings made standing; fasting; general anaesthetic; antibiotics at induction and clot-prevention measures
steps: Double incision: a curved incision along the lower border of each breast, following the line of the pectoral fold; the breast tissue and excess skin are lifted off the fascia of pectoralis major and removed, leaving a thin even layer of fat for a natural contour
Liposuction blends the edges and the axillary tail into the chest wall and armpit

Each nipple-areola complex is removed, trimmed to a smaller male size and replaced as a free graft lower and further out on the chest, held with a tie-over dressing; the graft has no blood or nerve supply of its own and must take from the bed beneath
Keyhole: a short incision at the lower border of the areola through which the tissue is removed, with no skin excised, for a small chest with elastic skin
Periareolar: an incision around the whole areola, with a ring of skin removed and a purse-string suture tightening the skin around it; in both the nipple stays on its own blood and nerve supply
Drains are placed, the incisions closed in layers and a compression binder or dressing applied
Breast augmentation (trans women): through an incision under the breast, around the areola or in the armpit, a pocket is made under or over pectoralis major and a silicone or saline implant placed
after: Home the same day or after one night; drains removed within days; nipple graft dressings left undisturbed for about a week
A compression binder worn for about 4-6 weeks; no lifting, reaching overhead or vigorous exercise during that time

Nipple grafts look dark and crusted at first and take weeks to settle; sensation in grafted nipples is largely lost and does not fully return, whereas periareolar and keyhole techniques, which keep the nipple on its own nerve supply, more often preserve some sensation, although it may still be reduced
Scar care (massage, sun protection, silicone tape as advised); a lump or change in the remaining tissue still needs assessment, and screening advice afterwards is individual
The tissue removed is sent for examination under the microscope; an unexpected abnormality is uncommon but is followed up in the usual way
chest-masculinisation.recovery: Desk work within 1-2 weeks and full activity by about 6 weeks; swelling settles over months and the scars fade and mature over about a year. Chest wall sensation is altered for months, and grafted nipples usually stay numb.
risks: Haematoma (blood collecting under the skin, the main early complication) and seroma (fluid), sometimes needing drainage
Infection and delayed wound healing, more likely in smokers
Partial or complete loss of a nipple graft, loss of pigment, or a nipple of unexpected shape or position
Loss of nipple sensation (expected with free grafts), scarring and keloid, asymmetry and bunching of skin at the ends of the scars ('dog ears'), with revision surgery sometimes needed

Residual breast tissue: chest surgery lowers but does not remove the possibility of breast cancer, so any new lump, skin change or nipple change still needs assessment, and screening advice after surgery is decided individually
alternatives: Chest binding with a purpose-made binder, with limits on hours, regular breaks and never while sleeping, to reduce skin, rib and breathing problems
Hormone therapy and social transition without surgery; not everyone wants surgery
Liposuction alone for small chests made up mainly of fat
For trans women: prosthetic breast forms, fat transfer, or continuing oestrogen, since breast growth continues for two to three years

UK Government: NHS population screening: information for trans and non-binary people

hysterectomy.name: Hysterectomy
hysterectomy.what: Removal of the uterus. A total hysterectomy takes the body of the uterus and the cervix and is the usual operation; a subtotal hysterectomy leaves the cervix in place; a radical hysterectomy, used mainly for cervical cancer, also removes the tissue beside the cervix (the parametrium), a cuff of the upper vagina and pelvic lymph nodes. The fallopian tubes are usually removed at the same time, and the ovaries may be removed with them (bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy) or left. The uterus can be taken out through the vagina, through keyhole incisions with or without a robot, or through a cut in the abdomen, depending on its size, the reason for surgery and previous operations. Periods stop afterwards and pregnancy is no longer possible.
why: Heavy menstrual bleeding that has not settled with medicines, a hormonal intrauterine system or ablation
Fibroids causing bleeding, pain or pressure on the bladder and bowel
Endometriosis or adenomyosis with pain that other treatments have not controlled
Prolapse of the uterus into the vagina, as part of a repair
Cancer of the uterus, cervix or ovary, and risk-reducing surgery in people with a high inherited risk
Gender-affirming surgery for trans men and non-binary people, sometimes with removal of the fallopian tubes and ovaries, which is decided individually, and sometimes before phalloplasty
before: A discussion of the alternatives and of the fact that the operation is permanent: fertility ends, so fertility preservation is raised first where it matters
Decisions agreed in advance about the ovaries (removing them before the natural menopause brings on a surgical menopause) and about keeping or removing the cervix
Blood count and group and save, with iron treatment beforehand if bleeding has caused anaemia; a pregnancy test where relevant
Ultrasound, and sometimes MRI, to size fibroids and plan the route; staging investigations when the operation is for cancer

Stopping smoking, weight and diabetes optimised, antibiotics at induction, clot-prevention stockings and injections, fasting and a general anaesthetic (some vaginal operations are done under a spinal)
steps: The bladder is emptied with a catheter and, for vaginal and keyhole routes, the legs are supported in the lithotomy position

Access is gained: an incision around the cervix from inside the vagina, small ports at the navel and lower abdomen with the abdomen inflated with gas, or a transverse incision along the bikini line (a midline cut for a very large uterus or cancer)
The round ligaments and the leaves of the broad ligament are divided and the bladder is pushed down off the front of the cervix and upper vagina

The blood supply is sealed and divided: the ovarian vessels in the suspensory ligament if the ovaries are being removed, or the ovarian ligament and tube if they are being kept, then the uterine arteries beside the cervix, where the ureter passes underneath the artery and is identified and kept clear

The uterosacral and cardinal ligaments are divided, the vagina is opened around the cervix and the uterus is delivered through the vagina, through the abdominal wound, or in pieces inside a retrieval bag at keyhole surgery

The top of the vagina (the vault) is closed and commonly suspended from the uterosacral ligaments to reduce later prolapse; the bladder, ureters and bowel are inspected, bleeding is checked and the wounds are closed

In a subtotal operation the uterus is divided at the level of the internal os and the cervix is left; in a radical operation the parametrium, a cuff of upper vagina and the pelvic lymph nodes are removed with the uterus
after: The catheter and any vaginal pack come out within a day, and walking starts the same day with clot-prevention injections and stockings continued as prescribed
Vaginal bleeding and discharge settle over a few weeks; nothing is put into the vagina and sex is avoided for about six weeks while the vault heals
Periods stop and pregnancy is no longer possible; hormone replacement is discussed when the ovaries have been removed before the natural menopause

Cervical screening is no longer needed once the cervix has been removed for a non-cancerous reason, samples from the vault are taken for a time after previous treatment for CIN, and screening continues as usual when the cervix has been left in place

Heavy or fresh vaginal bleeding, offensive discharge, fever, a hot or painful calf, breathlessness, or difficulty passing urine are reported to the surgical team or to NHS 111 without waiting for the follow-up appointment
hysterectomy.recovery: Hospital stay is usually one to five days, shortest after vaginal and keyhole surgery. Recovery takes about six to eight weeks after an abdominal hysterectomy and is often quicker after the other routes; driving resumes once an emergency stop is comfortable, and heavy lifting is avoided while the tissues heal. Tiredness, a swollen abdomen and low mood in the first weeks are common and settle.
risks: Bleeding, occasionally needing a transfusion, and haematoma at the vault
Infection of the wound, the vaginal vault, the chest or the urine
Injury to the bladder, the ureter or the bowel, uncommon but a recognised risk because the ureter runs just under the uterine artery
Venous thromboembolism (deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism), and the general risks of anaesthesia
Later problems: adhesions, vaginal vault prolapse, changes in bladder, bowel or sexual function, and an earlier menopause even when the ovaries are kept
Immediate surgical menopause when the ovaries are removed before the natural menopause, with hot flushes and long-term effects on bone
alternatives: For heavy bleeding: a hormonal intrauterine system, tranexamic acid, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory tablets, the combined pill or progestogens
Endometrial ablation, which destroys the lining but keeps the uterus
Myomectomy or uterine artery embolisation for fibroids, preserving the uterus
A vaginal pessary and supervised pelvic floor muscle training for prolapse
Watchful waiting: fibroids and heavy bleeding often improve after the menopause

phalloplasty.name: Phalloplasty and metoidioplasty
phalloplasty.what: Construction of a penis, most often as gender-affirming surgery for trans men and some non-binary people assigned female at birth, and occasionally after loss of the penis to injury or cancer. Phalloplasty builds a phallus from a flap of skin, fat and fascia moved with its own artery, veins and nerves, usually from the forearm or thigh, in a series of operations that can add a lengthened urethra, a glans, a scrotum with testicular implants and, later, an erectile device. Metoidioplasty instead releases the clitoris, enlarged by testosterone, to stand free as a small phallus in a single operation, with or without urethral lengthening. Gender incongruence is not a mental illness: the World Health Organization classifies it under conditions related to sexual health, and genital surgery is one option that some, not all, trans men choose.
why: Gender incongruence in trans men and some non-binary people who want male genital anatomy, standing urination or penetrative sex, after assessment under the WPATH Standards of Care

Metoidioplasty for those who prefer a smaller operation with no distant donor site and natural sensation and erection, accepting a small phallus; urethral lengthening, if wanted, may still need a graft and further stages
Phalloplasty for those who want a phallus of adult size that can later take an erectile implant
Reconstruction after loss of the penis through trauma or cancer surgery
before: Assessment by a gender identity service following the WPATH Standards of Care, usually after a period of testosterone therapy, which enlarges the clitoris (essential for metoidioplasty) and is continued around surgery

Discussion of fertility before any eggs are lost, with the option of storing eggs, because removal of the ovaries ends the supply of eggs and removal of the uterus ends the possibility of carrying a pregnancy; hysterectomy, with or without oophorectomy, and vaginectomy usually precede or accompany surgery when the urethra is lengthened
Permanent hair removal from the strip of forearm or thigh skin that will line the urethra, over the preceding months

Stopping smoking, which threatens flap survival; weight and diabetes optimised; the hand's circulation through the ulnar artery checked (Allen test, sometimes with Doppler ultrasound) before a forearm flap is planned

Choice of donor site and staging agreed with the surgical team: forearm flap (thin and sensate, with a visible scar), thigh flap (thicker, with a hidden scar, often needing a separate urethral lining) or metoidioplasty
steps: Hysterectomy (with or without oophorectomy) is usually done as an earlier operation; vaginectomy (removal of the vaginal lining and closure of the canal) is done at the stage when the urethra is lengthened, and a suprapubic catheter is placed to divert urine

The flap is raised: on the forearm a rectangle of skin, fat and fascia with the radial artery, cephalic vein and antebrachial cutaneous nerves; on the thigh a flap on the descending branch of the lateral circumflex femoral artery, which can stay attached to its pedicle
The flap is rolled into a 'tube within a tube': a narrow hair-free strip rolled skin-inward forms the urethra, and the wider outer tube forms the shaft

The phallus is fixed to the pubic region and the clitoris, stripped of its surface skin, is buried at its base; in a free flap the radial artery and cephalic vein are joined under the microscope to the femoral or deep inferior epigastric vessels, and the flap nerves to a dorsal clitoral nerve and the ilioinguinal nerve
The perineal urethra is lengthened with labia minora and vaginal mucosa and joined to the shaft urethra; the labia majora are brought together as a scrotum
The forearm donor site is covered with a split-thickness skin graft, usually from the thigh, and splinted; a thigh donor site is closed directly or grafted

Later stages, months apart: glansplasty to shape a glans, testicular implants in the scrotum and, once protective sensation has returned (typically a year or more), an inflatable or malleable erectile implant

Metoidioplasty: the clitoris is released from its suspensory ligament and the labia minora so that it stands free; the urethra may be lengthened with labial and vaginal mucosa and a scrotoplasty done in the same operation
after: About a week in hospital with the flap watched closely for colour, warmth and Doppler signal, since a blocked vessel threatens the whole phallus and needs an urgent return to theatre; bed rest at first
The suprapubic catheter stays for some weeks until the urethra has healed; a trial of voiding, sometimes with contrast imaging, checks for leaks before it is removed
The forearm is elevated and splinted while the graft takes; no weight-bearing or lifting with that arm for several weeks, followed by scar care and hand therapy
Testosterone continues; the person is taught to recognise a fistula (urine leaking from the perineum or shaft) or a slowing stream from a stricture and to report them early
Care follows the anatomy that remains: if the cervix has not been removed, cervical screening continues, and retained ovaries still need gynaecological care
phalloplasty.recovery: Recovery from each stage takes weeks, and the whole reconstruction is spread over a year or more. Sensation in a phalloplasty shaft returns from base towards tip over months to a year or more as the nerves regrow, and donor-site scars mature over about a year. Erotic sensation and orgasm are usually retained because the clitoris is preserved at the base. Standing urination follows successful urethral lengthening and penetrative sex follows an erectile implant. Metoidioplasty recovers in weeks and keeps natural sensation and erection, but the phallus is small.
risks: Urethral fistula and stricture, the commonest complications, especially after urethral lengthening; they may need further operations
Partial or complete flap loss from thrombosis of the joined vessels (uncommon but serious), or from wound breakdown, infection or haematoma
Donor site: a visible forearm scar, delayed graft healing, altered sensation, stiffness or cold intolerance of the hand
Later implant problems: infection, erosion through the skin and mechanical failure; testicular implants can extrude
Urinary tract infection, retention and a spraying stream
Venous thromboembolism after long operations and bed rest
alternatives: Metoidioplasty instead of phalloplasty, or phalloplasty without urethral lengthening (sitting to urinate), which avoids the commonest complications
Hysterectomy, chest surgery and hormone therapy without genital surgery; many trans men do not have genital surgery
Packers, stand-to-pee devices or prosthetics without surgery
The thigh rather than the forearm as donor site, avoiding a visible arm scar at the cost of a bulkier phallus

references.title: WPATH: Standards of Care for the Health of Transgender and Gender Diverse People, Version 8
UCSF Gender Affirming Health Program: Guidelines for the primary and gender-affirming care of transgender and gender nonbinary people
WHO: Gender incongruence and transgender health in the ICD

vaginoplasty.name: Vaginoplasty
vaginoplasty.what: Construction of a vagina and vulva, most often as gender-affirming surgery for trans women and some non-binary people, and occasionally for a vagina absent from birth (as in MRKH syndrome) or lost to cancer surgery. In the commonest technique, penile inversion, the skin of the penis, usually extended with a graft of scrotal skin, lines a canal made between the urethra and prostate in front and the rectum behind; the glans becomes the clitoris on its own nerve and vessels, the testes are removed and the urethra is shortened. Other techniques line the canal with peritoneum or a segment of sigmoid colon, or omit the canal altogether (vulvoplasty, also called zero-depth vaginoplasty). Gender incongruence is not a mental illness: the World Health Organization classifies it under conditions related to sexual health, and vaginoplasty is one option that some, not all, trans women choose.
why: Gender incongruence in trans women and some non-binary people who want female genital anatomy, after assessment under the WPATH Standards of Care
Congenital absence or underdevelopment of the vagina, for example in MRKH syndrome, or loss of the vagina to cancer surgery
Vulvoplasty for people who want the external anatomy without a canal, or for whom lifelong dilation is not practical
Revision of an earlier vaginoplasty for stenosis, loss of depth, granulation tissue or an unsatisfactory appearance
before: Assessment by a gender identity service following the WPATH Standards of Care: a settled decision, capacity to consent, other physical and mental health conditions well managed, and usually a period of gender-affirming hormone therapy where hormones are wanted and suitable (WPATH SOC8 suggests at least six months, and UK NHS pathways have typically asked for about 12 months)
Discussion of fertility, with the option of storing sperm, because removal of the testes ends sperm production
Permanent hair removal (electrolysis or laser) from the penile and scrotal skin that will line the canal, completed over the preceding months

Stopping smoking, with weight and diabetes optimised; oestrogen may be paused for some weeks around surgery to lower the risk of venous thromboembolism, but practice varies and many teams now continue it, especially transdermal preparations; the decision is made with the surgical team
Bowel preparation, fasting, general anaesthetic, antibiotics at induction and clot-prevention measures (compression stockings, anticoagulant injections)
steps: Under general anaesthetic the legs are raised in the lithotomy position and a urinary catheter placed; the testes and spermatic cords are removed through a scrotal incision (orchidectomy) unless this has been done earlier

The penile skin is freed from the shaft as a tube; the glans is reduced and kept on its dorsal neurovascular bundle to become the clitoris, the urethra is separated and shortened, and the corpora cavernosa are largely removed

A canal is dissected from the perineum between the urethra and prostate in front and the rectum behind, passing through the pelvic floor between the pubococcygeus muscles, with the rectal wall checked for injury
The penile skin tube, extended with a hair-free scrotal skin graft if extra depth is needed, is turned inside out and drawn into the canal to become its lining

The clitoris is set at the top of the vestibule with the shortened urethra opening below it; the labia majora are formed from scrotal skin and the labia minora and vestibule from penile or urethral skin
The canal is packed with gauze to hold the lining against its walls, the wounds are dressed and the catheter is left in place
In peritoneal or intestinal vaginoplasty a laparoscopic stage lines the canal with flaps of peritoneum or a segment of sigmoid colon, chosen where penile skin is scarce or as a revision
after: Several days in hospital, with bed rest at first; the packing and catheter are removed and the wounds checked before discharge

Dilation begins once the packing is out and follows a schedule that is frequent at first and reduces over months to a lifelong maintenance routine; regular rinsing of the canal clears debris; the lining is skin and does not lubricate with arousal, so lubricant is used for dilation and for sex

No penetrative sex for about three months, and no cycling, swimming or strenuous exercise until the wounds have healed; if oestrogen was paused it is restarted once the person is mobile, as the team directs

Follow-up with the surgical team, and pelvic floor physiotherapy if dilation is painful; the prostate remains, so prostate care continues, including PSA testing when indicated, interpreted knowing that removing the testes and suppressing androgens lower PSA, so a result in the usual range can be falsely reassuring; there is no cervix, so cervical screening does not apply; breast screening depends on how the person is registered with their GP: trans women registered as female are invited routinely, and those registered as male are not invited automatically but can ask their GP or the local screening service

Urgent review is needed for fever, heavy bleeding, increasing pain or swelling, inability to pass urine, or faeces or gas appearing in the canal, and for calf pain or breathlessness, which can signal a clot
vaginoplasty.recovery: Most people are back to normal daily activity within 6-12 weeks; swelling settles and the tissues soften over the following months, and full healing, with the final appearance and sensation, takes up to a year. Dilation continues for life, although the frequency can usually be reduced once healing is complete and for people who have regular receptive penetrative sex.
risks: Bleeding, haematoma, infection and wound breakdown along the labia or introitus, which usually heals with dressings
Granulation tissue, narrowing (stenosis) or loss of depth if dilation lapses, sometimes needing revision surgery
Injury to the rectum during the dissection and, rarely, a fistula between the canal and the rectum or urethra
Urinary problems (a spraying stream, retention, urinary tract infection) and altered or reduced clitoral sensation

Venous thromboembolism (deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism), guarded against with compression stockings, anticoagulant injections and early mobilisation, and sometimes by pausing oestrogen around surgery
Regret, which is reported to be rare
alternatives: Vulvoplasty (zero-depth vaginoplasty): the external anatomy without a canal, avoiding dilation
Orchidectomy alone, which removes the testes and the need for a testosterone-suppressing medicine
Hormone therapy, hair removal and other gender-affirming care without genital surgery; not everyone wants or needs surgery
Peritoneal or intestinal vaginoplasty where penile and scrotal skin are insufficient, or as revision after loss of depth
